promptText: What is the cleanest mental model for an agent orchestration loop, per the chapter?
options: A neural network whose layers correspond to loop iterations
A state machine whose fixed set of state slots (transcript, tools, iteration counter, budget) is transitioned by an LLM call instead of an engineer-written switch statement
A finite state grammar that has no notion of state at all
A pure functional pipeline that cannot branch based on runtime data
explanation: Everything you'd want from a hand-engineered state machine still applies — explicit terminal states, rejection of illegal transitions, observability — you have simply replaced the transition function with a model inference call.

promptText: What is the practical orchestration engineer's general guideline for choosing how much autonomy to grant the model?
options: Always maximize model autonomy for maximum flexibility
Pick the least amount of model freedom that still gets the task done, not the most
Autonomy level is irrelevant as long as every tool call is validated
Always default to a fully autonomous loop for production systems and constrain only if problems arise
explanation: This inverts the instinct of someone excited by what LLMs can do; more autonomy makes it harder to bound cost, prevent unwanted actions, and debug failures.

promptText: What key lesson did the AutoGPT/BabyAGI era of experimental autonomous agents teach the industry?
options: LLMs should never be given access to any tools under any circumstances
Autonomy without structural limits is not a feature, it is a liability — unattended, unbounded loops burned budget, wandered off-task, and rarely reached a satisfying conclusion
Fully autonomous loops always outperform structured orchestration patterns on complex tasks
Agent loops require reinforcement learning with a numeric reward signal to converge reliably
explanation: This lesson drove the industry back from 'let the model decide everything' toward giving the model bounded, well-scoped decisions inside an orchestration structure an engineer designed and can reason about.

promptText: What are the three steps of the ReAct loop pattern that most agent orchestration is built on?
options: Plan, Execute, Verify
Thought, Action, Observation
Generate, Critique, Refine
Encode, Retrieve, Decode
explanation: The model produces a thought about why it's about to act, an action (a tool call), and receives an observation (the tool's result), repeating until it decides it has enough information to answer.

promptText: Why must an orchestrator validate a requested tool call against a policy layer before executing it, rather than trusting the model's own reasoning?
options: The model's request is an input to your authorization logic, not a bypass of it — nothing in the mechanism itself guarantees a requested action is safe or permitted just because the model asked for it
Policy validation is only needed for tools that touch financial systems
Validation is purely a performance optimization with no safety benefit
The declared tool schema already guarantees the request is authorized
explanation: A well-built orchestrator rejects invalid or policy-violating calls and feeds the rejection back as an observation, rather than either crashing or blindly executing whatever the model requested.

promptText: What is the distinction between orchestration and choreography, borrowed from distributed systems?
options: Orchestration has no central controller; choreography has one central conductor directing every participant
In orchestration, one central component knows the whole process and tells each participant what to do next; in choreography, each participant reacts to events independently with no central conductor
Orchestration only applies to multi-agent systems; choreography only applies to single-agent loops
The two terms describe identical architectures with different naming conventions
explanation: Single-agent loops are almost always orchestrated, since one controlling loop decides what happens next; multi-agent systems can be built either way.

promptText: Why does total token cost for an N-iteration agent loop tend to grow closer to O(N^2) rather than O(N) in a naive implementation?
options: Because each tool call internally requires N separate model calls to complete

Because each iteration appends the previous tool result to a transcript that is never trimmed, so per-iteration cost itself grows roughly linearly with iteration count, compounding across all N iterations
Because the model's sampling temperature increases automatically with each additional round
Because embeddings for the full conversation history must be recomputed from scratch on every single turn
explanation: A naive implementation that never trims history means prompt size grows roughly linearly per turn, so total cost across N turns grows closer to quadratic — the mathematical reason 'just let it loop until done' is dangerous.

promptText: If each loop iteration has a constant per-turn probability p that the model decides the task is complete, why does this justify a hard maximum iteration ceiling rather than trusting the model's own stopping judgment alone?
options: Because a geometric distribution guarantees termination in exactly 1/p iterations every time

The number of iterations until termination follows roughly a geometric distribution with expected value 1/p, producing a long tail where a meaningful fraction of runs loop far longer than the mean — the same reasoning that justifies capping retries on a flaky network call
Because p is guaranteed to increase toward 1 as iterations accumulate
Token cost per iteration is fixed regardless of how many iterations occur, so this reasoning is irrelevant to cost
explanation: Even a modest per-turn continuation probability produces runs that loop far longer than average; this is exactly the behavior worth engineering a hard ceiling against.

promptText: Why should "tool execution failed due to a network timeout" be handled differently from "tool executed successfully but returned zero search results"?
options: They should always be handled identically because both technically qualify as errors

A zero-result search is valid, informative data that should be fed back to the model to adapt its next action; a timeout is an infrastructure failure that may warrant retry, abort, or alerting — collapsing both into one generic error path confuses the model and hides real outages from monitoring
Zero results should always immediately abort the entire orchestration loop
Network timeouts should always be presented to the model as if they were a final, confident answer
explanation: These are fundamentally different failure classes; conflating them into a single generic 'tool error' both confuses the model's reasoning and hides genuine infrastructure outages from your monitoring.

promptText: What does "resumability" mean for an orchestration loop, and why is it insufficient on its own to prevent duplicated side effects after a crash?
options: Resumability guarantees no duplicate side effects can ever occur, making additional tracking unnecessary

Resumability means persisting state after every step so execution can restart from the last checkpoint rather than the whole task; but if a resumed step might re-execute a non-idempotent action, the orchestrator also needs to track which side effects already committed, not just which model calls completed
Resumability only applies to purely read-only tool calls and is irrelevant to side-effecting ones
Resumability is a synonym for idempotency and requires no separate implementation
explanation: Resumability alone is not enough if a resumed step might re-execute a non-idempotent action like sending a confirmation email or charging a payment a second time.

promptText: In a fan-out/fan-in orchestration pattern, what new coordination problem does the fan-in step introduce?
options: Fan-in requires no additional logic beyond concatenating all branch outputs together
Deciding how long to wait for stragglers, what to do if one branch fails while others succeed, and how to merge results that may be redundant or contradictory
Fan-in eliminates the need for a shared state store across branches
Fan-in only applies when there is exactly one branch in the pipeline
explanation: None of this coordination comes for free simply from dispatching several branches at once; the orchestrator must explicitly decide timeout, partial-failure, and merge policy for the fan-in step.

promptText: Why does the chapter argue that DAG-based orchestration isn't inherently "more advanced" than a linear pipeline?
options: A linear pipeline is just a degenerate single-branch DAG; the real decision is whether the task's dependency graph actually has more than one branch — forcing a genuinely sequential task into a multi-node DAG adds observability and complexity without a matching benefit
DAGs are always superior because they support an unlimited number of nodes
Linear pipelines cannot be represented as DAGs under any circumstances
DAG orchestration requires an entirely different underlying model architecture than linear pipelines
explanation: A good engineer pushes back on the assumption that DAGs are automatically 'more advanced' — the actual question is whether the dependency graph has genuine parallelism to express.

promptText: Why can a prompt-injected instruction embedded in a single tool's output compromise more than just the one response, unlike injection confined to the original user message?
options: It doesn't — injected content is automatically discarded after each loop iteration

The poisoned content becomes part of the persistent transcript the model reasons from going forward, so it can steer every subsequent iteration's decisions rather than affecting just one response — validating and sanitizing tool outputs before they re-enter the loop matters as much as validating the initial call
Only the very first tool call in a loop can ever carry injected instructions
Injected tool output can only influence the final formatted natural-language answer, never intermediate tool-selection decisions
explanation: A poisoned search result or malicious webpage the agent reads does not just risk corrupting one response — it becomes part of the transcript and can steer every subsequent iteration of the loop toward unintended actions.

promptText: How can an attacker exploit runaway iteration behavior as a denial-of-service vector against an orchestrated agent, and what control mitigates it as both a cost and a security measure?
options: DoS against an orchestrated agent is only achievable through network-layer attacks, never through prompt content

A malicious or malformed input can push the loop toward its maximum iteration count on every request at full model and tool cost, draining budget even without ever producing an unsafe output; hard iteration and cost ceilings serve as both a cost control and a security control against this
Rate-limiting the API gateway alone is sufficient and no loop-level ceiling is needed
This risk is exclusive to fully autonomous loops and does not apply to any bounded orchestrator
explanation: Runaway resource consumption is a viable attack against your budget even without producing an unsafe output; the hard ceilings recommended for cost control double as a security control against this vector.

promptText: A team wants their support agent to have full autonomy to choose among forty available tools at every step, with no engineer-defined structure beyond the tool list itself. What is the staff-level critique and recommended alternative?
options: Full autonomy is acceptable as long as the underlying model is a frontier-class model

Full open-ended autonomy across a large tool surface maximizes the decision space exactly where mistakes are hardest to prevent and audit; the recommendation is to classify tools by risk, constrain which tools are reachable at which stage (e.g., a refund tool not callable before an order-lookup tool has run), and start with the least autonomous pattern that plausibly solves the task, widening freedom only based on measured limitations
The correct fix is simply adding more tools to cover additional edge cases the agent might encounter
The correct fix is reverting to prompted, text-based ReAct parsing instead of native tool calling
explanation: The history of early autonomous-agent projects shows unconstrained autonomy across a large tool surface reliably produces wandering, cost overruns, and unsafe actions as complexity grows; the staff-level response constrains reachability and risk rather than granting maximum freedom up front.
